Downe to thy pennance, thinke of thy whole youth, From the first minute that the wombe conceiv'd me To this full heaped houre I doe repent me, With heart as penitent as a man, dissolving, Of all my sinnes, borne with me, and borne of me; Dishonest thoughts and sights, the pathes of youth, So thrive in mercy as I end in truth.

Wasting his penitentiall times in plots, Acting more sinnes than he hath teares to we ̄ epe for them? Oh he's my protested servant, your sole Rivall. You'le make ̄ a hot Suitour of him anon? Oh pardon me ̄ my Lord, I had forgot, here 'tis, That is the same, and all that ere was his. I gave it you my Lord. Tymethes. I know not that my Lord. Twice set upon by Theeves within this Forrest Who rob'd me of my Cloathes, and left me these, Which better suite with my calamity: What fate pursues the good old King my husband, I cannot learne which is my worst affliction; Oh trecherous Lapirus! impious Nephew! All horrors of a guilty brest keepe with thee; Either poore Babes, you must pine here for food, Or have the wars drinke your immaculate blood. Oh flye ̄ , least life and honour be betrayd. Exit. If ever woman bore you. Let me disswade you from all hope of recompence Save thankes and prayers, which are the Beggers gifts, Generous sir, I was of Lydia once, as happie then As now unfortunate; till one Lapyrus, That trayterous villaine Nephew to the King Sought the confusion of his State and him; And with a secret Army guirt his Land, When peace was plighted by his enemies hand ▪ Little expecting such unnaturall Treason From forth a Kinsmans bosome; all admir'd But I his miserable Queene. Ile tell you all; for your so late attempt Confirmes you honest, and my thoughts so keepe you: I frighted at new warres, and his false breath, Chose rather with these Babes this lingering death. The truth of this sad story hath beene yours. Now, curteous sir, may I request your name, That in my prayers I may place the same, I heare you not sir, I desire you name. In this Forrest lurkes that abhorred villaine? His speedy death, I should forget all mercy, Had I but meanes fully to expresse my vengeance. No? by these Infants teares That weepe for hunger, I would throughly doe't. Oh where ̄ ? I see him not. Pray let me see him first. Puls off his false beard and kneeles. Lapirus! Oh fortunate revenge! now all thy villanies Shall be at once requited, thy countries ruine The King thy Vncles sorrow, my owne miseries, Shall at this minute all one vengeance meete. Alas, he doth submit, prayes, and relents, Who could wish more? none made from woman can, Small glory 'twere to kill a kneeling man: When he in penitent sighes his soule commends Thou send'st him to the Gods, thy selfe to th' fiends: But hearken to thy piteous Infants cryes, And th'are for vengeance, peace then, now he dyes. Ingratefull woman, he delivered thee From ravishment, canst thou his murthresse be? What's riches to thy honours? that rare treasure Which worlds redeeme not, yet tis lost at pleasure. Kill him that preserv'd that? and in thy rescue His noble rage so manfully behav'd: Rise, rise, he that repents is ever sav'd. I am better than my word, my word was death ▪ I pardon all Lapyrus. And onely to one penance I enjoyne thee For all thy faults past, while we here remaine Within this Forrest, this thy taske shall bee, To procure succour to my Babes and me. Th'art now growne good, here could I ever dwell, Were the old King, my husband safe and well. Exeunt. The peacefull'st reigne that ever Prince enjoy'd. Vnworthiest of all the joyes this houre brings forth. Your poore distressed Queene. Your joyes are perfect though he stand not there, And your wish blest behold a hopefull heire: Stand not amaz'd, 'tis Manophes. Happy houre, Heaven hath not taken all our happinesse; For though your elder met ill fate, good heaven Hath thus preserv'd your yonger for your heire.
Villaine ̄ and fugitive, where wilt thou hide Th' abhorred burthen of thy wretched flesh? In what disguise canst thou be safe and free, Having betray'd thy Countrey? base Lapirus. Earth stretch thy throate, take downe this bitter Pill, Loathing the hatefull taste of his owne ill. A Mother so enforc'd by pittilesse slaves? Let me redeeme my honour in her rescue, And in this deede my former basenesse dye. Who ere bore them monsters begot ̄ them; mercilesse damn'd villaines. You cannot give me that I have more neede of Than prayers; for my soule hath a poore stocke; There's a faire house within, but tis ill furnisht There wants true teares for hanging ▪ penitent falls, For without prayers souldiers are but bare walls: Whence are you? that with such a carefull charge, Dare passe this dangerous Forrest? Oh sinke into perdition, let me heare no furthe ̄ r, aside. Oh in her words I endure a thousand deaths. Ile put my death into her woefull hands. To adde some small content to your distresse, Know that Lapyrus, whom your miseries May rightly curse, and be revenged justly Lurkes in this Forrest equally distrest. These eyes did see him; and faith Lady, say If you should meete that worst of villaines here, That Treacher, Monster; what would you attempt? You would not, Queene. See yonder he comes. Here, take my sword, Are you yet constant? shame your Sex and be so; will you do't? Strike him through his guilt and trechery And let him see the horrors of his perjur'd soule, Are you ready? You see him now — now do't. Will misery yet a longer life afford; To see a Queene so poore, not worth her word? Man's nere past griefe, till he be past his breath. Doe not do't. And if I faile may the earth swallow me. Foule ̄ monster monger, who must live by that Which is thy owne destruction: Why should men Be natures bondslaves? Every creature else Comes freely to the Table of the Earth; That which for man alone doth all things beare ̄ Scarce gives him his true dyet any where. What spightfull winds breath here? that not a Tree Spreads, forth a friendly arme? distressed Queene, And most accursed Babes; the earth that beares you Like a proud mother, scornes to give you food: ha? Thankes fate, I now defie thee starveling hunger, Blest tree, foure lives grow in thy fruite, run tast it then, Wise men serve first themselves then other men. Oh me accursed and most miserable, Helpe, helpe, some Angell lay a listning eare To draw my cry up; none to lend helpe? oh Then pine and dye. Enter Clowne. A miserable wretch. No, no. Mocke not a man in woe, in a greene wound, Poure Balsome and not Physicke. I am no Surgeon friend, my names Lapirus. Lapirus is my name dost thou not know me? Torture me not, I prithee, I am that wretch; a villaine I was once; but I am now — Oh me most miserable and wretched creature! I now doe finde there's a revenging fate That doomes bad men to be unfortunate. [in the pit.] If you have humane formes to fit those voy ces And hearts that may be pierc'd with miseries groanes Sent from a fainting Spirit; pitty a wretch, A miserable man, Prisoner to darkenesse, Your charitable strengths this way repaire, And lift my flesh to the reviving Ayre. Millions of thankes and prayses. There's weight within keepes downe my soule and me ̄ Oh that astonishment had left me dead! Shame, sitting on my brow, weighes downe my he ̄ ad: Even thus the guilt of my abhorred sinne, Flasht in my face when I beheld the Queene ̄ . Within this forrest with her Babes distrest. Follow me then. My Lord, this Castle is but slightly guarded. Behold, the Tyrant maketh toward us. Some wretch on whom he wrought his Tyranny. Passion may spoyle us: sir, we oft have heard Of that old King his father; and that justly This Kingdome was by right due to his sway. Good. Our brother, a poore Pilgrime, that gives notice Of a Religious father that attends To beare us company in our Pilgrimage. Speranza. As full possest as ever, and as rich In Subjects hearts and voyces; we present thee The compleat sway of this usurped Kingdome.

My lov'd Lord? They shall be us'd my Lord, and any thing That comes to using, let it come to me. Exit. My Lady is scarce perfect in her thoughts How ere she fram'd a smile upon the Tyrant. I have some skill in faces, & yet they never were more deceit full; A man can scarce know a Baud from a Midwife by the face; An hypocriticall Puritan from a devout Christian If you goe by the face; well all's not streight in my Lady. She hath certaine crooked cogitations if a man had the liberty to search 'em: If ought point at my advice or performance, shee may fortu nately Disclose it: she knowes my mettle, and what it yeelds to an ounce, She cannot be deceiv'd in't: here's service, and secre ̄ cie, and no Lady can Wish more, beside a Monkey; she is assur'd of our faculties, there's none Of us all that stand her smocke Centinells, but would ven ter a joynt To doe her any pleasurable service, and I think thats as much As any woman desires — masse here she comes. Tis so me strange Physicke I know by the working. None that's good, Madam. The worst of all is, Madam, you are sad. Would I knew the meanes would make you so, I would turne my selfe into any shape or office To be the Author of it, sweete Lady. Thinke it? sfoote, you might sweare safely in that action And never hurt your oath — I nere fayld yet. Nay I know I did not. Not one, that's strange, I would 'twere put to me, Ile make it arrive safe what ere it be. Admit you love? why all's safe enough yet. Nay, now we are all spoyld Lady, I may looke for my braines in my Bootes— now you have put Home to me indeed, Madam; A stranger? there's a hundred Deaths in the very name, besides vantage. Faith no foole ̄ can fright me, Madam, commonly cal'd a stranger. Doe thee good, sweete Lady? as farre as I am able nere doubt it; Let me but cast about for safety, and Ile doe any thing, Madam, What is he? and his name? Hum, is that the most fortunate, spider catching, smocke wrapt Gentleman? What then? And is it possible a man should lye with a woman and yet not know her? And yet tis possible too—thanke my Invention, follow that game still. Lady, Madam, doe you heare? Have you leasure to swoune now, when I have taken such paines i' th' businesse? To take order for your safety, set all things right; why Madam? Why he sayes like a Gentleman every inch of him, And will performe the office of a gentleman; bring you to gether; Put you together, and leave you together: what gentleman can doe more? And all this safely? I by this hand will I, Or else would I might never doe any thing to purpose; If he have but the first part of a young gentleman in him. Tis granted Madam; I have crotchets in my braine That you shall see him and enjoy him, and he not know where he is, nor who it is. Why tis the least part of my meaning he should Lady. Doe you thinke you could possibly be safe and he know you? Why some of your yong Gallants are of that vaine-glorious and preposterous Humour, that if they lay with their owne Sisters you should heare them prate of't, This is too usuall, there's no wonder in't: what I have sayd I will sweare to performe, you shall enjoy him ere night And he not know you next morning. I am your creature Lady; pretty gold, And by this light me thinkes most easily earn'd, There's no faculty, say I like a Pander, and that makes so many Now adayes dye in the Trade: I have your gold Lady, And eke your service; I am one step higher, This office makes a gentleman a Squire. Exit. Masse here a walkes; I am far enough from my selfe, I challenge all disguises except drinking To hide me better; I give way to that, For that indeed will thrust a white gentle ̄ man Into a suite of mud, but whist I begin to be noted. Good your honours, your most comfortable charita ble releefe And devotion to a poore starre crost Gentleman. Ime bare enough already if it like your honour. Pox on thee? your yong gallants love to give no Almes ▪ But that that will sticke by a man, that's one vertue in them: He's not content to have my hat off, but he would have my hayre off too. Thanke your good Lordship. Good your honours! I have beene a man in my time. Kept goodly beasts, had 3. wives, 2. men uprising, 3. maides downe lying; oh good your kind ho nours. Perhaps your Lordship gets by it; Good your sweete honour ▪ Your Lordship has forgot since you were a Begger. But now you are in private, shut your purse, and ope ̄ n your eare sir. I am not literally a Begger, as Puritanicall as I appeare The naked Truth is you are happily desired. Of the most Sweete, delicate, divine, pleasing, ravishing creature That ever made mans wishes perfect. This for white and red sir, her honour and my oath sue for that pardon, You must not know her name nor see her face. She rather chuseth death in her neglect Than so to hazard life or lose respect. Let your will Subscribe to the sure meanes already wrought, She shall be safely pleas'd, you safely brought. Let me perish in this office else; and I neede wish No more damnation than to dye a Pander. Five is the fixed houre, upon to morrowes Evening. Neere to the further lodge. Else does there live no honestie but in Lawyers. Enjoy the sweetest Treasure in a woman. Exit. This is the farther Lodge, the place of meeting; The houre scarce come yet—well— I was not borne to this, There's not a hayre to chuse betwixt me and a Pander in this case, shift it off as well as I can: I doe envie this fellowes hap pinesse now; and could cut his throate at pleasure: I could ene gnaw feathers now to thinke of his downie felicity. I that could never aspire above a dayrie wench, the very creame of my fortunes; that he should bathe in Nectar, and I most un fortunate in Buttermilke, this is good dealing now, is't? Who's this? my Lord Mazeres discontent ▪ H' has beene to seeke me twice, and privately, I wonder at the businesse; I'me no Statesman; If I be, tis more than I know; I protest therefore I dare not call it in question; what should he make ̄ with me? Ile discover my selfe to him—if th' othe ̄ r come in the me ̄ ane time so I may be caught bravely, yet tis scarce the houre, Ile put it to the tryall. My lov'd Lord. The same my Lord. As far as life my Lord. Touch me then my Lord, and try my mettle. Well my Lord. Hum, what newes is here now? thou art wise farewell. By my troth I thinke it is a part of wisedome to take gold When it is offer'd, many wise men will do't: that I learnt Of my learned Councell: this is worth thinking on now. To kill Tymethes, so strangely belov'd by a Lady, and so mon strously detested by a Lord? here's gold to bring Tymethes, and here's gold to kill Tymethes. I, let me see, which weighes heaviest; by my faith I thinke the killing gold will carry't: I shall like many a bad Lawyer, runne my Conscience upon the greatest fee; who gives most is like to fare best. I like my safety so much the worse in this businesse in that Lord Ma zeres is his profess'd enemie: he's the Kings bosome, hee blowes his thoughts into him; and I had rather be torne with whirlewindes than fall into any of their furies. Troth as far as I can see, the wisest course is to play the knave, lay open this Venery, betray him; but see my Lord againe. My Lord? It will appeare I am so; be proud of your revenge be fore I name it; Never was man so fortunate in his hate, Ile give you a whole Age but to thinke how. Tymethes meetes me here. I meant at first to betray all to you sir: understand that my Lord. Then thus my Lord — he comes. My Lord Ile make your way. I but you'le play the better jumper of the two. I shall not jumpe so neere as you by a handfull. That is more hard; At a running leape you may give me a handfull. Nothing but put this hood over your head. You never went otherwise sir; for all folly is blind; Besides sir, when we see the sinne we act, We thinke each triviall crime a bloody fact. Servingmen alwayes follow their masters sir, There I leave you sir. Honestly, if protestation be not honest, I know not what to call it. Sheele trust you the worse for that sir. O sir, tis most common, He that loves women, is neere true to woman. Experience dayly proves he loveth none With a true heart, that affects more than one. Why then goodnight sir. He puts on the hood. Oh sir the better sports taste best in th' night, And what we doe in the darke we hate i'th'light. Oh sir, first try me, But we protract good houres, come follow me sir, Why this is right your sportive Gallants prize, Before they'le loose their sport theyle loose their e ̄ ye ̄ s. Exeu. You are at your— In my Lord, away, Ile helpe You to a disguise. And now your long lost eyes againe are found: good morrow sir. Puls off the hood. Rest here my Lord and you shall finde content, Catch your desires, stay here, they shall be sent. Valesta ? yes, the same; tis my Ladies pleasure, You give to me your coate, and vizarded attend without Till she employ you — so now, this disguise Serves for my Lord Mazeres, for he watches But fit occasion: Letcher, now beware, Securely sit and fearelesse quaffe and eate, You'le finde sowre sauce still after your sweete meate. Exit. This banquet from her owne hand received grace Her selfe prepar'd it for you; as appeares By the choyce sweetes it yeelds, able to move A man past sence, to the delights of love, I bid you welcome as her most priz'd guest, First to this banquet, next to pleasures feast. That speakes her sexes rarenesse, for to woman, The darkest path love treads is cleare and common; She wishes your content may be as great As if her presence fill'd that other seate. My Lord Mazeres caught the Office I can't but laugh to see how well he playes The Devill in a vizard; damne ̄ s where he crouches; little thinks the Prince Vnder that face lurkes his lives enemie, Yet he but keepes the fashion; great men kill As flatterers stab, who laugh when they meane ill. That cup hath quite dasht my Lord Mazeres. I would not taste of such a Banquet to feele that which followes it, For the love of an Empresse. Tis more dangerous to be a let cher Than to enter upon a breach; yet how securely he munches His thoughts are sweeter than the very meates before him: He little dreames of his destruction; His horrible fearefull ruine which cannot be withstood, The end of Venery is disease or blood The wind and tide serve sir, you have lighted upon A Sea of pleasure; here's your sayle sir, and your top streamer A faire wrought shirt and a night-cap. I, if you knew all sir. Five hundred Crownes in the shirt sleeve in gold. Tis my good Ladies pleasure, No Clouds ecclipse her bounty, she shines cleare, Some like that pleasure best that costs most deare; Yet I thinke your Lordship is not of that minde now; You like that best that brings a Banquet with it, and 500. Crownes. We jumpe somewhat neere sir. Oh sir, I nere knew any of your hayre but he was ab solute at the game. Nay sir I thinke you may see a thousand faces better cheap. Oh sir, you'le groape to purpose. Exit. Let me alone my Lord; doubt not Ile traine him: Perhaps sir I have the Art. The further lodge? Why so; I like one that will make an end of himselfe at few words; A man that hath a quicke perseverance in ill: A leaping spirit; hee'le run through horrors jawes To catch a sin; but to oretake a vertue He softly paces, like a man that's sent Some tedious darke, unprofitable journey. Corrupt is nature, she loves nothing more Than what she most should hate, there's nothing springs Apace in man but gray haires, cares, and sinnes. Exit Pleasures once tasted makes the next seeme worse. Oh sir, experience proves it, You came at first to enjoy what you nere knew, Now all is but the same what ere you doe. I have forgot a businesse to my Lord Mazeres, My safety to the King relyes upon't, You are in the house my Lord, this is the withdrawing Roome. No matter sir, as long as you have Feeling enough. Tis here in my hand sir, I must crave pardon, leave you here a while, But as you love my safety and your owne Remove not from this roome till my returne. Tis enough sir. Exit. Now I expect reward. Ha? what was that? there's a reward with a venge ance.

Is this he? I never knew the force of a desire Vntill this minute strucke within my blood; I feare one looke was destin'd to undoe me. He makes towards us: y'are Prince Tymethes? so I un derstand. Sir, y'are forgetfull, this is no place for Courtship, Nor we a subject for't, returne to your friend. Too cruelly in faith I put him by, Wine for our sonne Zenarchus, twas done kindly You sonne, and our best Visitant. Begin to me Zenarchus, Ile have't so. Ile prevent all loose thoughts, drinke to my selfe, My minde walkes yonder, but suspect walkes here. Make you yon stranger drinke. Rox. offers it him. I speake strange words against my fantasie. Thanks noble sir; I must be wary, my mind's dangerous. Ile pledge you anon sir. Gives Roxano the Cup. To you no lesse. Thankes to our sonne, Th' other tooke leave in silence, but left me To speake enough both for my selfe and thee. Tymethes ? that's his name, poore heart take heede, Looke well into th' event ere thou proceede: Love, yet be wise; impossible, none can; If ere the wise man claime one foolish houre Tis when he loves; he's then in follies power. I neede not feare the servants that ore-watch me ̄ Their faiths lye in my Coffers, in effect, More true to me then to my Lords suspect. The feares and dangers that most threaten me, Live in the party that I must enjoy, And that's Tymethes ; men are apt to boast; He may in full cups blaze and vaunt himselfe Vnto some meaner Mistresse; make my shame The politique Engine to beate downe her name, And from thence force a way to the Kings eares, Strange fate; where my love keepes, there keepe my feare ̄ s. It cannot be kept downe with any Argument, Tis of aspiring force; sparkes flye not downeward, No more this receiv'd fancy of Tymethes, I threaten it with my Lords Iealousy, Yet still it rises against all objections; I see my dangers, in what feares I dwell There's but a Planke ̄ on which I runne to hell, Yet were't thrice narrower I should venture on, None dares doe more for sinne than woman can. Misery of love — Roxano ? I am observ'd, What newes Roxano ? No? which is the bad! Indeede I am not merry. Troth I have that hope of thee, I thinke thou would'st Twere sinne to injure thee, I know thou didst not. But my trusty servant, This plot requires art, secresie and wit, Yet out of all can hardly worke one safety. Thou couldst not my Roxano — why admit I love, now I come to thee. I, but a stranger. I sayd I should affright thee. Hast thou the will? or dar'st thou doe me good? I, I, our safeties; which are meere impossibles, Love forgets all things but its proper objects. Tymethes, in a most unluckie minute Led hither by our Sonne in Law Zenarchus. Yet if he know me. I am undone. He must not know me; than I love no further; Although for not enjoying him I dye; My Lords pale jealousie does so orelooke ̄ me, That if Tymethes know what he enjoyes It may make way unto my Lords mistrust; Then since in my desire such horrours move Ile dye no other then the death of love. What sayes the man? And all this safely? How? shall he not know me? Thou art not onely necessary but pleasing, There, catch our bounty, mannage all but right, As now with gold, with honours weele requite. Exit. Oh my feare-fighting blood! are ̄ you all here. That's my wish, and my opinion Hath ever beene perswaded of your truthes, And I have found you willing t'all imployments We put into your charge. Will you to what I shall prescribe sweare secresie? To all things that you heare or see I sweare you all to secrecie; I poure my life into your brests, There my doome or safety rests. If you prove untrue to all Now I rather chuse to fall With losse of my desire, than light Into the Tyrants wrathfull spight: But in vaine I doubt your trust, I never found your hearts but just. On this booke your vowes arrive, And as in truth in favour thrive. Like Jewels all your vowes Ile weare. Here, take this Paper, there those secrets dwell, Goe reade your charge, which I should blush to tell. All's sure, I nothing doubt of safety now, To which each servant hath combin'd his vow. Roxano, that begins it trustily, I cannot chuse but prayse him, he's so needfull, There's nothing can be done about a Lady But he is for it; honest Roxano ; Even from our head to feete he's so officious, The time drawes on, I feele the minutes here, No clocke so true as love that strikes in feare. Exeunt.
